paras: The lynching of Dan Mann took place at Bartow, Florida, at an unstated date before September 1888. It is known only from a passing remark in a news item about a petition to pardon W. W. Willingham, a convicted murderer whose life Mann, as a juror, was said to have saved.

W. W. Willingham was tried for the murder of Wm. McGlaughlin at Fort Meade and was sentenced to life in the penitentiary "a year or two" before September 1888. According to the Lakeland Cracker, Willingham "would have been hung" had not one juror, Dan Mann, "insisted on a recommendation to mercy."

The same item describes Mann, in parentheses, as having been "subsequently lynched at Bartow." It gives no date, perpetrators, method or reason for the killing, and it does not state Mann's race. The wording places the lynching after Willingham's trial and before the item appeared, but no more exactly than that.
No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution in Mann's death appears in the coverage. The item itself was about something else: a petition for Willingham's pardon that was circulating at Lakeland.

The surviving mentions trace back to a single paragraph in the Lakeland Cracker. On September 11, 1888, the Tallahassee Weekly Floridian reprinted it under "State News" with credit to the Cracker, and the Savannah Morning News ran a lightly reworded version in its Florida column the same day. Neither paper gave the lynching a headline or any comment; in both it is a parenthetical clause inside a paragraph about clemency. The two versions differ only in small wording, with the Floridian saying the petition circulated "Monday" and the Morning News "last week," and "hung" against "hanged."

reader.title: Lynching of Dan Mann
bases: Both items say in passing that Dan Mann was 'lynched at Bartow' and give no other details [A1, A2].

The only evidence is a parenthetical saying Mann was 'subsequently lynched at Bartow' [A1, A2]. The word implies an extralegal killing, but nothing is said about who killed him, how many there were, or why, so the definition cannot be tested.
Both items go back to one Lakeland Cracker paragraph (A1 credits it; A2 repeats it nearly word for word next to another Lakeland item), and no direct report of the lynching was found [A1, A2].
